title: Gunmen kill Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez
description: A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.Polic
body: A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.Police said gunmen on a motorbike ambushed Camilo Rodríguez, 50, as he was travelling in his car north of the capital, San José, on Monday afternoon.The independent reporter earlier said he had been receiving death threats from drug trafficking gangs. Local media reported that it was the first murder of a journalist in more than two decades in Costa Rica. It comes at a time when transnational crime gangs are increasing their presence in the country, driving up its formerly low homicide rate. The president of the Costa Rican Journalists' Association, Yanancy Noguera, said that "all evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica - a person who published information about organised crime in the country".Rodríguez had been working as a journalist for several decades, both in radio and in print. Most recently, he had been uploading videos to social media in which he named public figures such as judges, business people and politicians, which he alleged were corrupt or had ties to known drug traffickers.In one of his videos, he alleged that the home of Costa Rica's President, Laura Fernández, had been constructed by a company that he said had links to a criminal gang.Fernández, who categorically denied any wrongdoing, took the journalist to court, accusing him of defamation. Reacting to his murder in a video message, the president strongly condemned the attack, calling it "a stain on freedom of expression". She added that she had instructed police to do their utmost to "punish Camilo's murderers".Rodríguez had also tried to stand for political office, seeking to run as the presidential candidate for the Costa Rican Renovation Party in 2021. However, his candidacy was rejected by the electoral authorities after the party failed to meet the necessary criteria required to file candidates.Costa Rica's Attorney General, Carlo Díaz, said that "silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society".

schema.headline: Gunmen kill Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez

title: Bilkis Bano: Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after Supreme Court bail for two convicts
description: The article has details that some readers may find disturbingA pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the
body: The article has details that some readers may find disturbingA pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back. The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap". On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken"."She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary." Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child. They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.How a Gujarat riot victim stood up to her rapistsIndia Supreme Court cancels release of 2002 riots rapistsIndia PM Modi's government okayed rapists' releaseHer attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief"."I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said."For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again." Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives". "I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

schema.headline: Bilkis Bano: Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after Supreme Court bail for two convicts

title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
description: The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.Once again, t
body: The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions."It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful."It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible. A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles. The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank. "It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk."What else could I do?" she shrugged. "It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

schema.headline: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge

title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
description: The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech
body: The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation. Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations". In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list. Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with ChinaIn the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred". They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

schema.headline: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed

title: Trump in Manila ahead of talks with Putin and Xi in China
description: US President Donald Trump has arrived in the Philippines' capital on the first leg of a trip to Asia, which will end in a meeting in China with its Pr
body: US President Donald Trump has arrived in the Philippines' capital on the first leg of a trip to Asia, which will end in a meeting in China with its President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin.A red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he walked off Air Force One in Manila. A band played one of his favourite songs, Y.M.C.A., before he was whisked away by helicopter to a hotel.Trump's first meeting at the Asean Summit was with US partners in the Quad - India's Narendra Modi, whom he described as a "very tough man", Japan's Sanae Takaichi, who "may be even tougher", and Australia's Anthony Albanese."Our countries are the four corners of the free, open, stable, prosperous Indo-Pacific," the US president said."We have outstanding relationships and co-ordinate closely... my phone is always open," Trump added.Many countries in South East Asia have been hit hard by Trump's tariffs and his war on Iran - but their exports to the US rose 30% last year thanks to the AI boom for which the region manufactures many of the components.The US is hoping to draw more countries here into its "Pax Silica" tech and AI ecosystem, and away from China.But China's huge influence in this region cannot easily be challenged, and certainly not in the few hours Trump is in the Philippines.Later on Tuesday, Trump signed a trade deal with Thailand alongside the country's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.The US is Thailand's largest export market, accounting for 24% of its total shipments this year.Trump then joined South East Asia leaders at a dinner, telling those gathered: "This is one of the world's most vibrant and productive regions filled with the tremendous potential."After an overnight stay in Manila, the US president will fly to Shenzhen in China to attend a summit of Asia Pacific leaders and have nuclear talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.Asked if he would also be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, Trump said: "If it's available, I would".

schema.headline: Trump in Manila ahead of talks with Putin and Xi in China

title: Carney looks to China as Trump tariffs squeeze Canada's car industry
description: Figure caption, Carney eyes 'other options' for embattled Canadian auto sector on China tripByNadine YousifSenior Canada reporterCanada's car industry
body: Figure caption, Carney eyes 'other options' for embattled Canadian auto sector on China tripByNadine YousifSenior Canada reporterCanada's car industry has become one of the clearest stress tests for Ottawa as it grapples with US tariffs on the sector.Now Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled that he is looking to China, where he is on a visit for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit (Apec), as part of the solution. But that avenue is not without controversy, and is once again drawing the ire of those close to Donald Trump. While in Cambodia earlier this week, Carney told reporters that Canada could turn to European and Asian carmakers to save its auto manufacturing sector if a trade deal with the US could not be reached.If Canadian auto workers are "not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities. "Canada's going to move forward either way," he said.He went on to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Tuesday for their second head-to-head in less than a year. The two talked of the importance of developing their relations, and Carney said they had agreed to further tariff cuts.Neither side mentioned vehicles specifically, though analysts suggest the issue will have been prominent in their minds.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Carney and Xi met on Tuesday to discuss cooperation and trade ahead of this week's Apec summitIn January, Carney said that opening the door to China's electric vehicles, external (EVs) could result in investment into Canadian-owned companies and the creation of manufacturing jobs in the sector. American tariffs on imports of Canadian-made vehicles have led to thousands of job losses in Canada and anxiety over the future, as 90% of cars made in Canada are shipped to and sold in the US.At the same time, China has been eyeing Canada as a potential entry-point to the North American EV market. Earlier this year, Canada announced that it would let in 49,000 EVs from China at a low tariff rate, with plans to raise that quota gradually to 70,000 by 2030.The move was a significant break from the US, which tariffs Chinese EVs heavily to protect domestic manufacturing.Peter Navarro, Trump's senior counsel for trade and manufacturing, warned the prime minister against cosying up to China in a post on X, external."Are u really threatening to play China off the US? This is offensive in the extreme," he wrote on Monday. "You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive."His comments were reposted by Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada.Image source, Maninder Sidhu/XImage caption, Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu toured a Chinese EV plant earlier this monthChinese EV manufacturers like BYD and Chery have already been lobbying the Canadian government for market access.Last week, Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu toured a Chery plant in China, external. He told reporters afterwards that Canadians could expect to see affordable Chinese EVs in Canada by early 2027.These moves come as the toll of US tariffs on Canada's auto sector has become harder to ignore.Stellantis, a multinational car manufacturer that made models like the Dodge Challenger in Canada, recently announced it would sell its assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario.The facility had been idle since 2023 for a planned retooling, but what was supposed to be a temporary shutdown became permanent after Trump's tariffs.The sale has led to speculation that a Chinese EV manufacturer could move into the facility, after Canadian media outlet CTV News reported, external, citing anonymous sources, that Stellantis was planning to lease back 25% of its plant to assemble "affordable" EVs.The idea is unpopular with Ontario Premier Doug Ford. In a letter to Carney, he warned against opening the door for Chinese EV kits to be assembled at the Brampton plant. China overwhelmingly builds its cars at home and ships them whole - or to be assembled in kits - overseas.Lynette Ong, director of the China Governance Lab at the University of Toronto, said introducing Chinese auto manufacturing in Canada would be "controversial" due to fears that Canadian jobs could be lost and that the North American industry could be eroded."We want to make sure they're hiring Canadian workers, that they are helping train Canadian workers and that they are transferring the technology over," Ong said.Carney noted there are "clear guardrails" in how Canada deals with China, including barring work on sensitive matters like artificial intelligence and critical minerals.Canada has also eyed other partnerships. It is notably pursuing associate member status with the EU, and had signed a free trade deal with the Philippines earlier this week. Just how much Canada is willing to embrace Chinese manufacturing, however, still depends on the outcome of ongoing US-Canada trade talks.Progress has been made in negotiations, Carney recently said, but differences remain. It is unclear if Trump and Carney will speak on the sidelines of the Apec summit later this week.Figure caption, Why China is winning the global EV race

schema.headline: Carney looks to China as Trump tariffs squeeze Canada's car industry

title: How Trump's chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in MayByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterAs US President Donald Trum
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in MayByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterAs US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of  data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market. But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.  This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".A blow to Asia's AI boomThis is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips. One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO. Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.  The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hubCountries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".A headache for ChinaThe new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models. Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months."This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

schema.headline: How Trump's chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China

title: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, A funeral was held for Fadda al-Fahidat in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta on TuesdayByYolande KnellMiddle East corre
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, A funeral was held for Fadda al-Fahidat in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta on TuesdayByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem and David GrittenA Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.All settlements are illegal under international law.Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Palestinian children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.Fadda's daughter-in-law, Nema al-Fahidat, told the BBC that she died from a single bullet wound to the head. "It destroyed her brain," she said.According to the Palestinian accounts, Fadda's son, Arafat, rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said, injuring several Palestinians, including Arafat."My husband, when he saw his mother, was not paying attention. He crashed into the vehicle. The vehicle was empty," Nema said."My husband got out of his car and tried to reach his mother and the injured young men. Then he was shot."She added: "We tried to gather the injured people and move them away from the settler. We brought them here. But he kept firing, firing, firing. Even after we had brought the wounded young men here and moved them away from him, he continued shooting."Nema said young Palestinians threw stones at the settlers after seeing what happened, but asked: "What can stones do against bullets?"Image source, ReutersImage caption, Medics say Palestinians and Israelis were wounded in the incident on Monday The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."Later, an Israeli military source said Fadda was shot by an Israeli civilian and that there was no evidence that she had been involved in the confrontation near her home.Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Israel's police force said it had opened an investigation, and that officers and forensic technicians had been collecting evidence and interviewing witnesses.The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.A BBC team saw settlers at the end of the street where Fadda was shot on Tuesday, as well as Israeli flags flying from four of the houses that they had moved into earlier this month.Image source, EPAImage caption, A group of settlers set up a new outpost in al-Duyuk al-Tahta earlier this month (file photo) In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".The UK government announced on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

schema.headline: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says

title: Komyshuvakha: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after strikes that killed 57
description: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72Figure caption, Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescuers af
body: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72Figure caption, Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescuers after ‘double-tap’ strikeByMerlyn Thomas BBC Verify correspondent and Paul BrownBBC VerifyUkrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue. The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.Image source, DSNSImage caption, Emergency service vehicles have also been targetedOleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.Image source, DSNSOleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.Fears of second strike heard on police radiosLocal people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.Figure caption, Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in UkraineBodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.Image source, Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesTrevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures. His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.Image source, SBUImage caption, The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kitBall and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

schema.headline: Komyshuvakha: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after strikes that killed 57

title: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers
description: After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.The Pan American Health Or
body: After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO,  announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to  persistent "gaps in vaccination". The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s. The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year."These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission. Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years. Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections. Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status"."Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans. "Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." In a post on social media, Kennedy said: "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles." "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he also said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment." The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards". The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths. But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems. The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns. An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials. Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database. Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics. The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge. President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine. Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates. "It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

schema.headline: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers

title: William and Catherine celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
description: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winner
body: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow."The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

schema.headline: William and Catherine celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai

title: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
description: Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia IrelandSarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv a
body: Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia IrelandSarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv and Ilya AbishevBBC News RussianUkraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014. The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.Image source, Anadolu Agency/Getty ImagesImage caption, Putin (centre) personally opened the Crimean Bridge by driving a lorry over it in May 2018In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands."We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."Image caption, Images show the damage to the Crimean Bridge from the overnight attackThe damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.  Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.The Kremlin said Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry. Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.Figure caption, Watch: BBC reports from Kyiv bridge hit by Russian attackIn Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

schema.headline: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine

title: Who to watch in race to run Spain after 29 November elections
description: Sánchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his s
body: Sánchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his sixth in 11 years - could be his toughest yet.Sánchez called the snap election eight months early, seeking to focus on resolving Spain's housing crisis, and vowing "an epic comeback of a progressive Spain" at the ballot box.But he and his party have been embroiled in a series of corruption scandals, a migrant crisis in Spain's Ceuta exclave on the Moroccan border and two deadly rail disasters nine months apart. The most recent tragedy claimed 69 lives at Urda on 28 October and overshadowed the start of the campaign.The Socialist leader has been written off in politics before, only to stage comebacks, notably in 2017 and 2023.He can point to a projected 2.6% annual growth in the Spanish economy in 2026, fuelled by tourism, but the graft cases against his inner circle and family are not going away.José Luis Ábalos, who was transport minister in Sánchez's government, is now serving a 24-year prison sentence for accepting kickbacks, meanwhile leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, faces trial over allegations of influence peddling and embezzlement while his brother, David Sánchez, has been banned from public office for nine years for misconduct. Both deny doing anything wrong.In a defiant message, Begoña Gómez made her first party speech at the Socialist campaign launch, calling for the backing of Spanish women, "because when women step forward, all of Spain follows".Sánchez's fate could be sealed by the rise of Abascal's anti-immigration, populist Vox - with opinion polls putting them in a comfortable third place and taking votes from the Socialists.Abascal, 50, denies his party is far-right and has succeeded in bringing Vox into the mainstream, attracting record ratings on one of Spanish state TV's primetime entertainment shows during the campaign.Repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain are big themes for Abascal, who has accused Pedro Sánchez of promoting an "act of invasion" with his policies.He has promised to use the Spanish navy to defend the national borders and "send a message to the world that there is no room here for all of Africa and all of the Americas".The Vox leader joined the PP aged 18, becoming a local councillor first and then an MP in the Basque regional parliament.His political trajectory was closely shaped by his family's experience of threats and intimidation by Basque militant group Eta. Both his father and grandfather, who held public office, were targeted because of their political roles.He left the conservatives in 2013, founding Vox the following year and becoming a Spanish MP in 2019, when Vox became the first hard-right party in decades to establish a significant presence in Congress.Vox has adopted the Trump-inspired slogan "Make Spain Great Again" and advocates a strongly centralised vision of the country strongly opposed to the independence movement in Catalonia.Critics have described the party's ideology as reminiscent of aspects of the era of dictator Francisco Franco era, which Vox rejects.Isabel Díaz Ayuso, 48, has been president of the Madrid region since 2019 and has become one of the most influential figures within the People's Party. She leads one of the PP's strongest electoral bastions, with conservatives having ruled the region for the past 31 years.Ayuso has built a distinct political profile that often sets her apart from the party establishment. Her direct communication style and informal use of language have helped her connect with voters and attract significant media attention.Her tenure has not been without controversy. Her partner has been the subject of a judicial investigation relating to alleged tax offences and document forgery, allegations he denies.Opposition parties have also questioned the Madrid regional government's purchase of a luxury penthouse for official use. Critics have challenged the rationale behind the acquisition, while regional authorities have maintained that it was intended as a government workspace.Socialist Carlos Cuerpo, 46, was chosen by Pedro Sánchez to take charge as interim transport minister after the Urda rail disaster and has become key to his election team. Cuerpo climbed the ranks through the economy ministry and became minister of economy, trade and business in 2023. He has been ranked as best-regarded politician among the Spanish public, according to the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), and, when asked about his political ambitions has called himself "a team player, and I am committed to the team".In the same light, Sánchez has said: "I believe politics is a team sport; on the opposing team we have Feijóo and Abascal, and on my team we have Carlos Cuerpo."Catalonia's Socialist president Salvador Illa is also one to watch. He served as Spain's health minister during the Covid pandemic and some have viewed him as a potential successor as Socialist leader, even though he has backed Sánchez to remain as leader.

schema.headline: Who to watch in race to run Spain after 29 November elections

title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
description: Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its l
body: Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Thursday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.She has her alarm set for 05:00 GMT, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is". She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.   This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers."As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said."Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include  banning players.GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither have Sony nor Microsoft.Louise Wooldridge from Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases."Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game."So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video. "The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter the cost or extra effort.Additional reporting: Kris Bramwell

schema.headline: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6

title: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody
description: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custodyImage source, FacebookImage caption, Lt Col Brandon Carrol
body: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custodyImage source, FacebookImage caption, Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested on 10 November ByHafsa Khalil and Daniel SandfordUK correspondentA US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police. Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to. "We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The US serviceman is understood to have been based at Imjin Barracks in GloucestershireOn Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress.""These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners."Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said. "This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take."Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

schema.headline: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody
